title: Ellington calls himself Pop and enjoys Chuckles
summary: Chuckles' vibraphone and operatic scat pleased Ellington; Green tells him his partner is a big fan and Ellington says call me Pop.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: It was very classy, very classy. That's why I say rich, you know, enriching. See, Duke Ellington's appearances, you know, on these tours -- because I mean America couldn't keep this man very long -- he was in such great demand with that orchestra, see. I mean, there was other countries that wanted him on radio and so forth, make records -- recording companies, you see. And he was like in and out of America, you see. His home base was up here in the Cotton Club. Whenever he was here -- he didn't do too many one-nighters, because they had went through all of that -- these one-night-stands, you see. The most popular show business in them days was repeat performance, and that was the strongest point in the profession, repeat performance, you see. They had places -- they had like theaters -- they called them circuits, you know, and they would name the show like unit, or something like that, you know. And they would have the charter -- the charter was the charter -- all reservations was in unison, you see. And you made the best of friends because the world, especially America -- because they was proud

of themselves, you know. They had forgotten that they was poor. Of course, they had gotten back some of their returns and their, you know, their fortunes or whatever their savings were, you know, and they was back into their own speculation, see.

But that was the most thrilling thing, see. I mean, of course, now my partner, Chuckles -- like he had to learn these -- he was playing this musical instrument and I think Mr. Ellington -- he was kind of proud of that -- of course, the vibraphone was something like the piano, in a way, you know. And he could (unintelligible) scat operatic, you see. Operatic singing, but he was doing it in scat. And he was very funny -- it was comical. They had him doing this jazz so you -- it just got to be loved -- this fellow, my partner -- he got to be loved by everyone. Back stage, there, I mean, we used to go by his dressing room, you know, and he would be in there and I'd try to talk to Mr. Ellington, you see. I'd try to say something nice (unintelligible). I used to say, "Mr. Duke"-- Ellington, you know. I'd say, "You know, my partner is a big fan of yours." He'd say, "Call me Pop." I'd say, "Well, Pop, my partner is a big fan -- and me too -- is a big fan of yours, especially (unintelligible)" I mentioned one of his records somewhere -- I didn't hear -- I know the people were dancing because they used to dance by music. People would hear music coming over a sound system, you know -- they had a tendency to go into their dance, you know. That's the way -- I was trying
to be impressive to him, you know. I guess he was tickled about it, you know. It was a great experience, you see, and he always inspired everyone that I know, especially that show, you see.
